In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the in vitro transcription and replication of Sendai viral RNA and its defective interfering particles (DI) in cell-free systems.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Sendai virus cytoplasmic protein pool contains all the proteins required for viral RNA replication and that these proteins are not synthesized de novo in vitro.
Sendai virus RNA can be replicated and encapsidated in a cell-free system, but only if the cell-free system is supplemented with the soluble protein fraction.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Sendai virus replication is dependent on a soluble protein fraction containing viral and nonviral proteins, and this soluble protein fraction is not present in purified virions.

the Sendai virus cytoplasmic protein synthesis machinery is able to replicate both the 50S wild-type genome RNA and the 14S DI genome RNA in the absence of new protein synthesis, but only if the template RNA and associated proteins are provided.
the in vitro replication system for Sendai virus and DI-H RNA is a useful model for the study of the replication of RNA viruses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the replication of Sendai viral RNAs can be studied in vitro, and this system will be useful for investigating the molecular mechanisms of RNA replication.
the Sendai virus genome RNA replication system in vitro can be used for studying the mechanism of RNA replication and the role of the viral proteins in this process.
the Sendai virus replication system is amenable to the in vitro study of RNA replication and the identification of the proteins and RNAs that are required for the process.
